channel.title: Worldview Weekly
channel.description: A weekly global counterweight reading feed: concise, analytical, low-noise, and deliberately broader in perspective than The Economist.

item.title: The ‘Stability-Instability Paradox’ Comes for Markets — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 27, 2026 · medium (~15 min)

Emma Ashford and Matthew Rojansky argue that the resilience of global energy markets during the Iran war may itself encourage dangerous complacency. Inventories, rerouted supply and policy buffers softened the shock, but those buffers are finite.

Counterweight: Treats markets as institutions operating under geopolitical uncertainty rather than as automatically self-correcting systems.

item.title: Why Are Yields on U.S. Treasury Bonds Rising? — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 28, 2026 · medium (~12–15 min)

A clear account of the renewed rise in long-term U.S. Treasury yields and the interaction among deficits, inflation expectations, monetary policy and investor confidence.

Counterweight: Keeps fiscal policy, market structure and political choices in the same frame instead of treating bond moves as isolated financial noise.

item.title: Yes, We’re in an AI Bubble. Just Look to 1980s Japan. — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 28, 2026 · medium (~15 min)

The piece compares today’s AI investment boom with late-1980s Japan, arguing that real technological progress can coexist with excessive valuations, capital misallocation and unrealistic expectations about future returns.

Counterweight: Resists the false choice between “AI is transformative” and “AI is a bubble”; both can be true.

item.title: Ditching Chinese Rare Earths Is Hard. Just Ask Japan. — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 24, 2026 · medium (~12–15 min)

Christina Lu uses Japan’s long effort to diversify away from Chinese rare earths as a warning for Washington. Even after years of stockpiling, overseas investment and alternative-supply projects, Japanese firms remain exposed to China in key heavy rare earths.

Counterweight: Complicates simple reshoring and de-risking narratives by emphasizing industrial lead times, chemistry, financing and entrenched supply chains.

item.title: Russia and North Korea Are Scrambling Trump’s Alliance Strategy — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 28, 2026 · medium (~15 min)

Donggak Heo argues that deeper Russia–North Korea military cooperation undermines Washington’s attempt to divide security burdens neatly by region. Pyongyang’s role in Ukraine increasingly links European and Northeast Asian security.

Counterweight: Challenges the assumption that allied strategy can be cleanly divided into separate theaters while adversaries integrate across them.

item.title: The SCO’s Diminishing Usefulness for India — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 28, 2026 · medium (~12–15 min)

C. Raja Mohan argues that the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation offers India increasingly limited strategic value as Chinese influence inside the grouping grows, even while summit diplomacy remains useful.

Counterweight: Complicates narratives that treat SCO- and BRICS-style forums as coherent anti-Western blocs.

item.title: Peacemaking Is Power Politics Again — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 25, 2026 · medium (~15 min)

Comfort Ero and Richard Gowan argue that the post-Cold War model of institutionalized peacemaking has weakened as major powers return to bargaining, coercion and ad hoc diplomacy. Conflict mediation is migrating toward regional powers and influential capitals rather than disappearing.

Counterweight: Avoids both nostalgia for the old multilateral order and fatalism about its decline.

item.title: How the Meta Settlement Could Change the Internet — The New Yorker
item.description:
The New Yorker · August 29, 2026 · medium (~15 min)

A landmark settlement between Meta and U.S. states imposes substantial new safeguards for young users and creates a potentially important precedent for regulating social platforms through product design and business incentives.

Counterweight: Frames platform governance as an issue of incentives and architecture, not merely individual pieces of harmful content.

item.title: Could Data Centers Swing an Election in Wisconsin? — The New Yorker
item.description:
The New Yorker · August 28, 2026 · medium (~15 min)

The rapid expansion of AI data centers has become a potent Wisconsin political issue, combining concerns about electricity, water, subsidies, corporate power and local control.

Counterweight: Shows AI becoming ordinary mass politics through infrastructure and land-use conflicts rather than abstract debates about model capability.

item.title: Notes From Russia’s Literary Underground — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 29, 2026 · medium-long (~18 min)

A report on Russian writers and publishers working around censorship through exile networks and publishing abroad, showing how literary life persists under tightening political control.

Counterweight: Approaches authoritarianism through cultural institutions and the practical survival of intellectual life, not only through elite politics.

item.title: A Book as Big as the War — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · August 29, 2026 · long (~20 min)

A substantial review of a large new history of 1942, using one pivotal year to connect the Pacific and European wars and to reconsider familiar narratives about the conflict’s turning points.

Counterweight: A deliberately historical selection that widens the issue beyond immediate policy arguments and current events.

item.title: The End of the European Summer — The New Yorker
item.description:
WORLDVIEW BACKGROUND · The New Yorker · August 24 & 31 issue · long (~30–35 min)

Eric Klinenberg reports on how European cities are redesigning streets, public space, shade, vegetation and cooling systems as extreme heat becomes a structural urban problem.

Why it pierces through: It turns climate adaptation into a concrete question of urban design, public goods and inequality.
